research.summary: Quiver Quantitative exposes a REST API at https://api.quiverquant.com with an OpenAPI 3.0.3 spec (55 paths) at https://api.quiverquant.com/docs/schema.json, bearer-token auth, and datasets grouped into Tier 1 (congress/house/senate trades, congress holdings and net worth, PAC donors, Trump trades, gov contracts, lobbying, revolving-door lobbyists, off-exchange/dark-pool short volume, Polymarket trades, adjusted daily OHLCV from 2014) and Tier 2 (Form 4 insiders, 13F holdings/changes, top shareholders, exec comp, patents, app ratings, Quiver news). API plans are Hobbyist $30/mo ($300/yr, Tier 1), Trader $75/mo ($750/yr, Tier 1+2), Startup $250/mo list (commercial use, <$1M revenue) and Enterprise; the $25-30/mo website Premium is a separate product with no API key, and no free API tier is listed. The official PyPI package `quiverquant` (v0.2.6, 2026-05-07) is a single-file requests wrapper that is minimally but recently maintained; the official tutorials repo uses raw requests instead. Quiver runs an official remote MCP server at https://mcp.quiverquant.com/ (18 tools, same API key; Hobbyist gets 10, Trader all 18) and several community MCP servers exist. Numeric rate limits are not published anywhere official (only "Higher Rate Limits" on commercial plans); congressional data is legally delayed up to 45 days (PTR due within 30 days of notification, max 45 days after trade). WSB/reddit and Twitter endpoints still exist as routes but are absent from the current spec and pricing, so their status is unverified. The main backtest pitfall is that the API returns the current revised snapshot, not point-in-time vintages: signals must be timestamped on ReportDate/Filed or Quiver_Upload_Time (never TransactionDate), ReportDate can be null, records get revised (last_modified), and the ExcessReturn/PriceChange fields embed future returns.

facts.claim: The API base URL is https://api.quiverquant.com (OpenAPI 'servers'), spec is OpenAPI 3.0.3 titled 'Quiver API' v1, 55 documented paths, all GET except POST /beta/token/login/ and /beta/token/logout/; endpoints are tagged 'Tier 1', 'Tier 2', 'public', 'enterprise', 'internal', and 'New Constructs Ratings'.

Auth per the OpenAPI spec is a single security scheme 'WebPlatformTokenAuth' of type http / scheme bearer. Quiver's own tutorials repo sends 'Authorization: Bearer <key>', while the official PyPI client (v0.2.6) and QuantConnect's downloader send 'Authorization: Token <key>'; both header forms come from Quiver-authored code, but which are accepted was not verified with a live key.

Unauthenticated requests return HTTP 401 {"detail":"Authentication credentials were not provided."}; a bad token returns 401 {"detail":"Invalid token."}; nonexistent routes return an HTML 404. No rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit, Retry-After) were present on 401 responses; server header is cloudflare.
facts.source: Direct curl probes of https://api.quiverquant.com/beta/live/congresstrading and /beta/live/doesnotexist123 on 2026-10-06

facts.claim: Tier 1 (Hobbyist) endpoints include: /beta/live/congresstrading (params normalized, representative), /beta/bulk/congresstrading (ticker, date YYYYMMDD, bioguide_id, representative, nonstock, normalized, page, page_size, version V1|V2; 'Returns the full history'), /beta/historical/congresstrading/{ticker}, /beta/live/housetrading, /beta/live/senatetrading, /beta/historical/housetrading/{ticker}, /beta/historical/senatetrading/{ticker}, /beta/live/congress_stock_holdings, /beta/live/congress/politicians, /beta/bulk/congress/politicians, /beta/bulk/corporatedonors, /beta/historical/corporatedonors/{ticker}, /beta/bulk/trumpstocktrades, /beta/live/govcontracts, /beta/live/govcontractsall (date, page, page_size), /beta/historical/govcontracts/{ticker} (quarterly totals), /beta/historical/govcontractsall/{ticker}, /beta/live/lobbying (date_from, date_to, page, page_size), /beta/historical/lobbying/{ticker}, /beta/live/revolvingdoor, /beta/live/offexchange ('yesterday's off-exchange activity', page_size max 20000), /beta/historical/offexchange/{ticker} (date), /beta/historical/dailyprices/{ticker} (OHLCV + adjusted + corporate actions, 'from 2014 onward', date_from/date_to), /beta/live/polymarkettrades.

Tier 2 (Trader) endpoints include: /beta/live/insiders (params ticker, date, uploaded, limit_codes, page, page_size), /beta/live/sec13f, /beta/live/sec13fchanges, /beta/live/topshareholders/{ticker}, /beta/historical/executivecompensation/{ticker}, /beta/live/allpatents (date_from/date_to, 'max 30 day range'), /beta/historical/allpatents/{ticker}, /beta/live/patentdrift, /beta/live/patentmomentum, /beta/live/appratings ('last week'), /beta/live/quivernews. Enterprise-only tagged: /beta/live/bill_summaries, /beta/live/legislation, /beta/live/congressholdings, /beta/live/rss, /beta/strategies/holdings. Internal-tagged (not for customers): /beta/live/cnbc, /beta/live/flights, /beta/coins, /beta/funds, /beta/companies, /beta/tickerdata, eventsbeta.

WallStreetBets/reddit and Twitter datasets are NOT in the current OpenAPI spec or on either pricing page, yet /beta/live/wallstreetbets, /beta/historical/wallstreetbets/{ticker}, /beta/live/wsbcomments and /beta/live/twitter still answer 401 'Invalid token' (route exists) rather than 404, and the official Python client 0.2.6 still ships wallstreetbets(), wallstreetbetsComments(), twitter(), spacs(), flights(), political_beta() and cryptoComments() methods. Whether any current plan returns data for them is unverified. QuantConnect separately still sells a Quiver WSB dataset (since Aug 2018, 6,000 equities, nightly 4am, $5/mo).

Congress trading response fields: Representative, BioGuideID, ReportDate ('Date the transaction was reported'), TransactionDate ('Date the transaction took place'), Ticker, Transaction (Purchase/Sale), Range, Amount ('Lower bound of transaction size'), House, Party, District, last_modified ('Date that Quiver last updated the details of this transaction'), TickerType, Description, ExcessReturn, PriceChange, SPYChange. The bulk endpoint's V2-style schema adds Traded, Filed ('Disclosure date'), Quiver_Upload_Time ('Time that transaction was scraped and processed by Quiver'), Status, Subholding, Comments, Chamber, Trade_Size_USD, State.

Insider (Form 4) fields: Ticker, Date (transaction date), Name, AcquiredDisposedCode, TransactionCode, Shares, PricePerShare, SharesOwnedFollowing, fileDate ('Time that the transaction was filed (and became publicly available)'), uploaded ('Time that the transaction was uploaded by Quiver'), officerTitle, isDirector, isOfficer, isTenPercentOwner, isOther, directOrIndirectOwnership. Lobbying Date is 'Date that the lobbying spend was reported'; gov contracts have Date ('Announcement date') and action_date; off-exchange has Date, OTC_Short, OTC_Total, DPI; 13F changes Date is 'Filing date (ms since Epoch CST)' plus ReportPeriod.

Official Python package is `quiverquant` on PyPI: latest 0.2.6 uploaded 2026-05-07, author Chris Kardatzke (chris@quiverquant.com), deps pandas + requests, python>=3.6, MIT; repo https://github.com/Quiver-Quantitative/python-api (59 stars, last push 2026-05-07, default branch main, only 4 files: quiverquant.py, setup.py, README, LICENSE). Release history shows 0.2.2 on 2023-06-09 then nothing until 0.2.3-0.2.6 in May 2026, i.e. minimally maintained with a recent refresh. The client hardcodes an X-CSRFToken header and uses 'Token' auth.

Quiver also publishes https://github.com/QuiverQuant/quiver-api-tutorials (MIT, pushed 2026-09-24) with backtest scripts (insider_buying_monthly.py, revolving_door_lobbying.py) that use raw requests with Bearer auth, filter insiders to TransactionCode == 'P', time signals on fileDate / DatePosted / reported Date, shift target weights by one period for execution lag, and use /beta/historical/dailyprices/{ticker} for adjusted prices; the revolving-door script notes 'Hobbyist plan is enough'.

facts.claim: API pricing (api.quiverquant.com/pricing): Hobbyist $30/mo or $300/yr ($25/mo) — Congress Trading, Congress Stock Holdings, Politician Net Worth, Corporate Donors, Government Contracts, Corporate Lobbying, Off-Exchange Trading, Donald Trump Stock Trades, Polymarket Trades, Daily Equity Prices, Revolving Door Lobbyists, '10 of 18 Quiver MCP Tools', 'No Commercial Use Rights'. Trader $75/mo or $750/yr ($62.50/mo) — all Hobbyist plus Insider Trading, Hedge Fund Activity, ETF Holdings, Top Shareholders, Corporate Patents, Executive Compensation, App Ratings, Quiver Newsfeed, 'All 18 Quiver MCP Tools', no commercial use. Startup $250/mo list ($125/mo first year with automatic 50% discount; annual $1,250 first year vs $1,500 list) — Commercial Use Rights, 'only offered to companies with under $1m in annual revenue', all Hobbyist & Trader datasets. Enterprise — contact for pricing, commercial rights for >$1m revenue. Partner add-on New Constructs ratings $199/mo or $2,189/yr. 'Priority Support & Higher Rate Limits' and 'Commercial Use & Redistribution' are marked only for the Commercial column.

Website Premium ($30/mo or $300/yr, i.e. $25/mo) and the API are separate subscriptions: 'Premium doesn't include an API key' and an API key does not unlock Premium site features. The MCP setup page says to 'Ensure the account has an active API subscription'; no free API tier appears on the API pricing page. Third-party listings citing an API tier 'starting at $10/month' (apievangelist) are inconsistent with the current pricing page and should be treated as stale.

Historical data: no separate 'historical' add-on exists; historical endpoints carry the same Tier 1/Tier 2 tags as live ones and /beta/bulk/congresstrading 'Returns the full history of transactions'. Daily prices run 'from 2014 onward'. QuantConnect's mirror of Quiver congress data starts January 2016 and covers ~1,800 US equities. The only explicit lookback restriction found is /beta/live/allpatents 'max 30 day range'.

No numeric rate limits are published: the OpenAPI spec has zero mentions of rate limits/429, the Terms of Service do not mention them, and the pricing page only lists 'Priority Support & Higher Rate Limits' as a commercial-plan perk (implying tiered, unpublished limits). The apis.io 'Quiver rate limits' profile (10 req/min & 1,000/mo free; 100/min & 100,000/mo pro; 1,000/min enterprise) explicitly labels its numbers 'scaffold values to be replaced with published provider limits' and must not be relied on.

Legal disclosure delay: under the STOCK Act, Members/senior staff must report securities transactions over $1,000 on a Periodic Transaction Report 'within 30 days of notice of the transaction, but in no case later than 45 days after the transaction'; late PTRs incur a $200 late fee (with a 30-day grace period) and late filings are common. Corporate insiders must file Form 4 within two business days. Lobbying (LDA) filings are quarterly with roughly a 20-day posting lag per Quiver's own tutorial comment.

Quiver's ingestion latency after filing is not quantified officially; the congress-trades product page says you 'receive detailed information on new trades as soon as they are filed through financial disclosures', the site banner says 'within moments of being filed', and QuantConnect's mirror is 'Updated nightly at 4am'. The Quiver_Upload_Time (congress) and uploaded (insiders) fields give the actual time Quiver made each record available.

An OFFICIAL Quiver MCP server exists: remote endpoint https://mcp.quiverquant.com/, configured either with header 'Authorization: Bearer <your-api-key>' (same key as REST) or via 'npx -y mcp-remote@latest https://mcp.quiverquant.com/', and also available through the Claude connector directory with OAuth sign-in to a Quiver account. 18 tools: search_datasets, get_congress_trades, get_congress_politician, get_congress_legislation, get_corporate_donors, get_gov_contracts, get_lobbying, get_trump_trades, get_political_exposure, get_dark_pool, get_insider_trading, get_institutional_holdings, get_ticker_ownership, get_patents, get_executive_compensation, get_quiver_newsfeed, get_ticker_full_picture, compare_tickers. Hobbyist unlocks 10 (politics/government + dark pool), Trader all 18; 'Tool access is enforced on your API key'. Works with Claude Code/Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT.

Community MCP servers: jsconiers/quiver-quant-mcp (Python/FastMCP, 16 tools incl. WSB and offexchange, env QUIVER_API_TOKEN, pushed 2026-06-19, 1 star); bolshchikov/quiver-mcp (Python stdio, env QUIVER_ACCESS_TOKEN, MIT, pushed 2025-06-07, 2 stars); pipeworx-io/mcp-quiver (TypeScript, 4 tools, MIT, pushed 2026-09-26, 0 stars); nimblebraininc/mcp-quiver (Python, 8 tools, env QUIVER_API_KEY, MIT, listed on PulseMCP 2026-03-28). All are low-adoption; the official remote server supersedes them.

Backtest pitfall (point-in-time): the API returns the current revised snapshot, not historical vintages. QuantConnect's open-source Quiver downloader documents the issues: 'ReportDate might be null, but we use it for setting the EndTime... So if it doesn't exist, we don't know when the data was made available to us' (rows with null ReportDate are dropped), 'It's a data bug when the report date is greater than the last modified date', and 'The upload date can be greater than report date. It means the report date was incorrect and an update has fixed it'. For records older than their dataset start they simply set UploadDate = ReportDate, i.e. true availability time is unknown for older history.

Additional backtest pitfalls from the schema: Amount is only the lower bound of a reported range; TickerType includes non-stock assets (QuantConnect keeps only null/'Stock'/'ST'; the bulk endpoint has a nonstock flag); ExcessReturn, PriceChange and SPYChange are computed 'since the transaction date' and therefore leak future returns if used as features; last_modified shows records are retroactively edited; live endpoints return only 'most recent' rows while per-ticker historical endpoints require one call per ticker (use paginated /beta/bulk/congresstrading for full history). Quiver's own 'Congress Buys' strategy page (weekly rebalance, weighted by reported purchase size, backtest from 2020-04-01) does not state whether entries use transaction or disclosure date.

Terms of Service (last updated June 25, 2026): Quiver Data is 'licensed exclusively for personal, non-commercial use' on standard plans; prohibited to 'redistribute, republish, resell, sublicense... or otherwise make Quiver Data available to any third party' or use it 'in connection with any business, investment advisory, research, or data analytics service' without an enterprise agreement; content 'may be lagged, outdated, or otherwise inaccurate'. Personal swing trading on a Hobbyist/Trader key is within scope; offering signals to others is not.

QuantConnect resells Quiver datasets (congress trading, insider trading, WSB, wikipedia, gov contracts) at $5/month cloud access, updated nightly at 4am, with open-source LEAN data-source repos (e.g. QuantConnect/Lean.DataSource.QuiverQuantCongressTrading, pushed 2026-06-18) — an alternative integration path if backtesting on LEAN.

recommendations: Plan choice for a retail swing trader: Hobbyist ($30/mo) covers congress/house/senate trades, holdings, gov contracts, lobbying, dark-pool short volume, PAC donors and adjusted daily prices; upgrade to Trader ($75/mo) only if Form 4 insider trades, 13F changes, patents or exec comp are part of the strategy. Both are non-commercial, which is fine for personal trading but not for selling signals.

Integrate via the official remote MCP server (https://mcp.quiverquant.com/ with 'Authorization: Bearer <key>') for Claude Code/agent use, and a thin custom requests client generated from https://api.quiverquant.com/docs/schema.json for the pipeline; do not build production code on the single-file `quiverquant` PyPI package (hardcoded CSRF header, 'Token' auth, 3-year maintenance gap).
Send 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' as the spec says, but test 'Token <key>' as well on first run since Quiver's own client and QuantConnect use it; log which works and pin it.

Build your own point-in-time ledger: pull full history once via paginated /beta/bulk/congresstrading (and /beta/live/insiders with the uploaded filter), store ReportDate/Filed, TransactionDate, last_modified and Quiver_Upload_Time, then snapshot new/changed rows daily going forward so later backtests can replay what was actually known on each date.

Timestamp every signal on max(ReportDate or Filed, Quiver_Upload_Time) plus one trading day of execution lag — never on TransactionDate; drop rows with null ReportDate; treat records older than the earliest Quiver_Upload_Time as having unknown true availability and apply a conservative lag (e.g. ReportDate + 1-2 days).

Exclude ExcessReturn, PriceChange and SPYChange from features (they embed returns after the transaction date); filter TickerType to stock-only; treat Amount as a range lower bound; for insiders keep TransactionCode == 'P' open-market buys and use fileDate, mirroring Quiver's own tutorial.

Because rate limits are tiered but unpublished, implement client-side throttling with exponential backoff on HTTP 429, cache responses locally, and prefer bulk/paginated endpoints over per-ticker historical calls for universe-wide pulls; if exact quotas matter, email info@quiverquant.com (contact in the OpenAPI info block).

Do not plan around Quiver WSB/reddit or Twitter sentiment until verified with a live key — the routes exist but are undocumented and absent from all current plans; QuantConnect's $5/mo Quiver WSB dataset is the only documented current source.

Use /beta/historical/dailyprices/{ticker} (adjusted OHLCV from 2014, FIGI-mapped, corporate actions) for a consistent price series, or a dedicated price vendor for the execution leg; control survivorship bias with historical index constituents as Quiver's revolving-door tutorial does.
open_questions: What are the actual numeric rate limits per plan (requests/minute and monthly quota)? Nothing official is published; needs a live key (inspect response headers) or a reply from info@quiverquant.com.

Do the WallStreetBets, wsbcomments, Twitter, SPAC, flights and political-beta routes return data on any current paid plan, or are they retired? They respond 401 (not 404) but are missing from the spec and pricing.
Are both 'Bearer' and 'Token' Authorization schemes accepted? The OpenAPI spec says bearer; Quiver's own Python client and QuantConnect's downloader send 'Token'.
How far back is Quiver_Upload_Time populated for congressional trades (i.e., how deep is true point-in-time history), and does Quiver offer historical vintage snapshots/bulk exports for backtesting?
What does version=V2 on /beta/bulk/congresstrading change in the response (the schema merges Traded/Filed/Quiver_Upload_Time with ReportDate/TransactionDate fields)?
Is there any free API tier? The MCP setup page implies an API subscription is required and the pricing page lists none; the '$10/month' figure in third-party catalogs appears stale.

Quiver's Congress Buys/Sells strategy pages and Congress Backtester do not disclose whether entries use disclosure date or transaction date — confirm before trusting their published backtests as a benchmark.

research.summary: "Liquid Trade" almost certainly refers to Liquid (liquid.trade), legal entity LiquidX AI, Inc. (Delaware C-corp), a New York startup founded in 2025 by ex-Two Sigma researcher Franklyn Wang. It is not a brokerage: it is a non-custodial, no-KYC mobile/web interface that aggregates on-chain perpetual-futures venues (Hyperliquid, Lighter, Ostium) so retail users can take leveraged perp positions that track stocks, indices, FX, commodities, crypto, pre-IPO names and prediction markets 24/7. It does offer a real, documented Claude/MCP connector called Co-Invest (https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp, Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1 PKCE, scopes read/trade) launched May 26, 2026, plus an autonomous "Co-Invest Computer" mode with configurable risk limits and a $10k paper-trading mode; a public REST API exists but is undocumented and Discord-gated. It is not registered with FINRA, SEC, CFTC or NFA (its Terms say so explicitly; BrokerCheck and EDGAR searches return zero hits), and "stocks" on it are perpetual contracts, not shares. Other entities with similar names (the defunct FTX-owned Liquid/Quoine exchange, Australian CFD broker Liquid Brokers whose principal's AFSL was cancelled in Feb 2026, a gold-signals Discord called Liquid Trade Room) are distinct and less likely to be what a US retail swing trader means in 2026.

facts.claim: Liquid (liquid.trade) is operated by LiquidX AI, Inc., a Delaware C Corporation; Terms of Service are governed by Delaware law.

Liquid describes itself as 'a non-custodial trading app for crypto perpetuals, stocks, pre-IPO companies, commodities, FX, indices, and prediction markets, open 24/7 with up to 50x multipliers' and routes each market 'to a specialist venue', unifying 'one login, one balance, one set of markets, and one price feed'.

Liquid aggregates decentralized perpetual-futures venues Hyperliquid, Lighter and Ostium into one non-custodial app; founder Franklyn Wang (ex-Two Sigma); ~10-person team in New York City; $7.6M seed led by Paradigm with General Catalyst (closed March 2025, reported Nov 3, 2025); Liquid takes 'a small additional fee on top of trades'.

Liquid closed an $18M Series A (announced April 28, 2026) co-led by Neo and Left Lane Capital, with Haun Ventures, K5 Global, SV Angel, AntiFund and Sunflower Capital; press describes 'up to 200x leverage in certain jurisdictions'.
Team page states Liquid has 'raised $25.6M+ from investors including Neo, Left Lane, Paradigm, General Catalyst' and team comes from Two Sigma, Bloomberg, D.E. Shaw, Gauntlet.

'Stocks on Liquid are perpetual futures that track the share price' (users do not own shares); only crypto spot is actual underlying tokens. Max leverage per docs: crypto perps 40x, stock perps 20x, commodities 25x, indices 50x, FX 50x; all perp markets trade 24/7/365 including when stock exchanges are closed.

Co-Invest MCP server: primary URL https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp (https://coinvest.liquid.trade also works); transport 'Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 (authorization code + PKCE)'; no API keys; OAuth scopes are `read` ('market data, portfolio, account state') and `trade` ('placing and managing orders behind confirmation').

MCP tool categories exposed: 'market analysis, market search, news, technical indicators, portfolio, open orders, order execution, TP/SL, position management, prediction market orders, deposits, leaderboard, and referrals'. Docs say to 'list tools to discover the current catalog' after OAuth; exact tool names/schemas are not published.

Claude Code setup: `claude mcp add --transport http co-invest https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp` then `/mcp` to sign in; claude.ai: Settings > Connectors > Add custom connector, name 'Co-Invest', URL https://coinvest.liquid.trade; Claude Desktop/stdio clients use `npx mcp-remote https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp`; Cursor .cursor/mcp.json uses {"url":"https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp"}.

Standard Co-Invest requires per-order human confirmation: 'Claude renders a confirmation card showing the symbol, direction, size, multiplier... Press Confirm or Cancel. That is the only way an order reaches the exchange.'

Co-Invest Computer is an autonomous mode 'designed for code-agent clients that run loops, schedules, and multi-step plans' that executes within configured limits without per-order approval; limits include max notional per order and per day, max multiplier, mandatory stop-loss on every position, optional symbol allowlist, daily order caps, and expiry for goals/strategies; execution modes are simulation, staged orders, or live orders.
Paper trading: 'a simulated $10,000 balance running against live market data', available through Co-Invest by asking to 'switch to paper mode'; paper settings are scoped per connector.

A public REST API exists but is undocumented: docs say 'A public REST API is available; contact Discord for access'. The docs index (llms.txt) has no pages for API, API keys, WebSocket, or rate limits.

Co-Invest launched May 26, 2026 in ChatGPT and Claude (also Grok, Meta Muse, iMessage per vendor page); covers 500+ markets; 'available in all 50 U.S. states and most other jurisdictions' with sanctions exclusions; CEO Wang cited SEC/CFTC guidance including the CFTC no-action letter for Phantom as support that Liquid does not need broker or exchange registration.

Fees: perps carry a 0.05% Liquid fee on top of venue fees (tier-0 all-in taker 0.095% / maker 0.065%); Ostium-routed stocks/FX/commodities/indices add 5 bps Liquid fee on top of venue (stocks 5 bps venue); no Liquid add-on for Lighter-routed markets; prediction markets free to open, 0.9% on close; withdrawals $1 flat (USDC); Co-Invest itself is free.
Minimum position: '$10 of collateral in the app and Chrome extension, and $15 through Co-Invest'; withdrawals in 'minutes, with a flat $1 network fee and no lockups'.

KYC: 'Liquid does not require identity verification to create an account or trade with crypto'; accounts are self-custodial embedded wallets secured by passkeys/biometrics with no seed phrase. Terms of Service nonetheless reserve the right to perform KYC.

Regulatory status: Terms of Service state 'We do not operate any exchange, designated contract market, swap execution facility, broker-dealer, introducing broker, futures commission merchant, clearing organization, sportsbook, gaming platform, or prediction-market venue.' No SEC/FINRA/CFTC/NFA registration is claimed anywhere on the site or docs.
FINRA BrokerCheck firm search for 'LiquidX' returned total:0; SEC EDGAR full-text search for "LiquidX AI" (2024-01-01 to 2026-10-06) returned 0 hits.

The CFTC Phantom no-action letter (March 17, 2026) is Phantom-specific and conditioned on orders routing to 'registered designated contract markets (DCMs) or through registered futures commission merchants (FCMs) or IBs' with joint-and-several liability undertakings; Hyperliquid, Liquid's main venue, is not a CFTC-registered DCM and geo-blocks US IPs under its own terms. Liquid's reliance on that letter as precedent therefore does not map cleanly onto its documented venues (analyst inference, not a verified legal finding).

Homepage disclaimer: 'Liquid (liquid.trade) is not affiliated with Liquid Brokers, liquidmarkets.org, or the former Liquid exchange.' Official domains are liquid.trade, app.liquid.trade, docs.liquid.trade (301-redirects to docs.tryliquid.xyz), coinvest.liquid.trade.
Security: one named smart-contract audit by Zellic (PDF at /LiquidMax-Zellic-Audit-Report.pdf, no date shown). Trustpilot: 3.4/5 from only 3 reviews, profile claimed May 2026.
iOS app 'Liquid — Trade like the 1%' (App Store ID 6744045653, v2.27.1) lists seller as HyperSports, Inc. with LiquidX AI, Inc. in the copyright; Android package is xyz.trade.rn.

Alternative candidate (ruled out): Liquid (Quoine) crypto exchange at liquid.com was FTX-owned and halted all withdrawals Nov 15, 2022; the PyPI package `liquidcli` (last release v0.0.25, Aug 27, 2019, by 'Suzuito') targets api.liquid.com for that defunct exchange, not liquid.trade.

Alternative candidate (ruled out): Liquid Brokers / Liquid Markets Pty Ltd is an Australian forex/CFD broker; ASIC cancelled AFSL 220383 of its principal Pulse Markets Pty Ltd on Feb 11, 2026, and that licence covered wholesale clients only.
Alternative candidate (unlikely): 'Liquid Trade Room' (liquidtraderoom.com) is a gold-signals Discord service claiming a 73% win rate; it offers no API, data feed, or execution.
No active product was found at liquidtrade.io, liquidtrade.com or liquidtrade.ai; searches for those domains return only liquid.trade results.
facts.source: WebSearch for 'liquidtrade.io OR liquidtrade.com OR liquidtrade.ai'

recommendations: Confirm with the user that they mean Liquid at liquid.trade (LiquidX AI, Inc.); it is by far the most likely match for a 2026 US retail trader, and it has a working Claude connector, but it is a leveraged perpetual-futures interface, not a stock broker.

Make the product reality explicit before designing anything: 'stocks' on Liquid are perp contracts routed to offshore/on-chain DEXs (Hyperliquid, Lighter, Ostium); the user never owns shares, there is no SIPC/FINRA protection, the operator is unregistered by its own Terms, and the regulatory basis the CEO cites (Phantom no-action letter) assumes CFTC-registered venues that Liquid's documented venues are not. A swing trader wanting regulated US equity execution and data should look at a FINRA-registered broker API (e.g., Alpaca, Interactive Brokers, Tradier) instead or in addition.

If the user proceeds, connect via the documented path: claude.ai custom connector at https://coinvest.liquid.trade, or `claude mcp add --transport http co-invest https://coinvest.liquid.trade/mcp` in Claude Code; grant only the `read` scope initially and run everything in paper mode ($10k simulated, live prices) before touching `trade`.

For a baseline 'AI swing trader' program, treat Co-Invest as the execution/portfolio layer only: after OAuth, call tools/list to capture the live tool catalog (docs do not publish tool names or schemas), and use Co-Invest Computer's hard limits (max notional per order/day, max multiplier, mandatory stop-loss, symbol allowlist, daily order cap) as the risk envelope; start in 'simulation' or 'staged orders' mode.

Do not rely on Liquid as the market-data backbone: its data is scoped to its own listed perp markets and the docs expose charts/technical indicators but no bulk historical OHLCV, WebSocket, or rate-limit documentation. Pair it with a dedicated historical/fundamental data source (Quiver Quant for alt-data, plus an OHLCV provider) for backtesting and pattern recognition.

If REST access is required, ask in Liquid's Discord (the only documented route) and get endpoint, auth, and rate-limit details in writing before building on it; otherwise assume MCP is the only stable public interface.

research.summary: Surveyed (as of 2026-10-06, via official docs/PyPI/GitHub where reachable) the Python building blocks for a US-equity AI swing trader. Backtesting: vectorbt OSS (1.1.1, Sept 2026) and vectorbt PRO are the strongest for fast daily-bar sweeps with built-in rolling/expanding/purged walk-forward splitters; NautilusTrader (1.231.0 final 1.x, 2.0.0rc6) and Lumibot (4.6.4) give backtest-to-live parity (IB only for Nautilus; Alpaca/IB/Tradier/Schwab for Lumibot); QuantConnect LEAN is Apache-2.0 but live/paper needs a paid plan ($84/mo Researcher) and has no native walk-forward; backtrader upstream is dead (last PyPI 2023-04); zipline-reloaded and backtesting.py are maintained but backtest-only with no walk-forward. Data: EODHD ($19.99/mo, ~60k US delisted symbols via delisted=1) and Massive/ex-Polygon ($29/mo Starter, tickers active=false) are the practical survivorship-bias-aware options; Alpaca Basic (free, 200 req/min, 2016+) is good for execution-side data but has only partial delisted coverage; yfinance is personal-use-only per Yahoo ToS and widely rate-limited. Brokers: Alpaca paper is free with no funded account; Tradier has a free sandbox and $10/mo Pro; IB requires TWS/Gateway (50 msg/s) and its official MCP (July 2026) only drafts trades; Webull OpenAPI has an auto-approved sandbox; Schwab has no sandbox and 7-day refresh tokens. LLM frameworks (TradingAgents v0.6.0, ai-hedge-fund, FinRL, FinGPT, FinMem, AgenticTrading) are all research/simulation-first; 2025-26 benchmarks (StockBench, Look-Ahead-Bench, OpenPM) show most LLM agents fail to beat buy-and-hold and that standard LLMs leak future knowledge, so point-in-time data discipline is essential. Quiver Quant is a paid alt-data API ($30/mo Hobbyist, no free tier, 18 MCP tools); 'Liquid Trade' (liquid.trade) is a non-custodial crypto perp-DEX aggregator offering leveraged synthetic 'stock' perps with an MCP server, not a US stock brokerage, and its US eligibility could not be verified.

recommendations: Minimal solo-dev stack (why): (1) DATA — EODHD Historian ($19.99/mo) as the research backbone for 30+ years of daily bars plus the delisted=1 symbol list (the cheapest verified survivorship-bias-aware source); Massive Starter ($29/mo) is the alternative if you prefer REST ergonomics and an official MCP server (tickers active=false gives delisted names). Use Alpaca Basic (free, 200 req/min) only for execution-side quotes/bars since its delisted coverage is partial and history starts 2016. Skip yfinance for anything beyond throwaway prototypes (personal-use ToS, 429s, no delisted data). Add Databento only if you later need intraday/tick fidelity.

(2) BACKTEST — vectorbt open-source (1.1.1, Apache-2.0+Commons Clause) for daily-bar swing research: vectorized sweeps over hundreds of tickers/parameters in seconds and RollingSplitter/ExpandingSplitter for walk-forward; upgrade to vectorbt PRO if you want purged k-fold/CSCV and the Rust engine. Validate the final strategy in an event-driven engine that can also run it live: Lumibot (4.6.4, GPLv3) if you execute on Alpaca/Tradier, or NautilusTrader (wait for 2.0 stable or pin 1.231.0) if you execute on Interactive Brokers. Avoid backtrader upstream (unmaintained since 2023) and treat zipline-reloaded/backtesting.py as research-only (no live bridge, no walk-forward).

(3) BROKER — Start on Alpaca paper (free, no funded account, same alpaca-py code for live); graduate to Alpaca live or Tradier Pro ($10/mo, sandbox 60 req/min, trading 60 req/min) for commission-free equities. Choose IB (TWS API via ib_async, paper port 7497, 50 msg/s cap) only if you need margin/short locates/international; note IB's official MCP cannot submit orders. Webull's auto-approved sandbox is a viable fallback; Schwab is the worst fit for automation (no sandbox, 7-day refresh tokens, manual approval).

(4) AGENT LAYER (Claude) — Use official MCP servers rather than hand-rolled wrappers: alpacahq/alpaca-mcp-server (paper default), massive-com/mcp_polygon, mcp.alphavantage.co, and Quiver's 18 MCP tools (Hobbyist $30/mo exposes 10) for congressional/insider/lobbying signals. Study TradingAgents v0.6.0 and ai-hedge-fund for prompt/role design, but keep the LLM as an analyst/feature generator (news, filings, alt-data scoring, regime commentary) and keep position sizing, stops and order submission in deterministic Python with hard risk caps, because StockBench/OpenPM show most LLM agents do not beat buy-and-hold and Look-Ahead-Bench shows standard LLMs leak future knowledge in backtests.

(5) PATTERN RECOGNITION / STRATEGY INTEGRATION — Build classic pattern and indicator features (breakouts, pullbacks, relative strength, volatility regimes) in vectorbt/pandas; if adding ML, use gradient-boosted models trained strictly walk-forward with purging/embargo on point-in-time data (EODHD delisted lists or Massive date-snapshots) and benchmark every model against buy-and-hold and a simple momentum baseline. Reserve FinRL (DRL) for experimentation only — its PyPI release is from 2022 even though the repo is active.

(6) ON 'LIQUID TRADE' — Do not wire it in as the equities venue: liquid.trade is a non-custodial crypto perp-DEX aggregator whose 'stocks' are leveraged synthetic perpetual contracts (no share ownership, funding rates, up to 50x), its MCP explicitly pushes all risk onto the local agent, and US eligibility/KYC could not be verified. If you want its MCP at all, treat it as read-only market-sentiment input, never as an execution target for a US-equity swing book.

(7) BASELINE PROGRAM SHAPE — A fully data-capable baseline is: a nightly ingest job (EODHD/Massive -> Parquet/DuckDB, including delisted symbols), a vectorbt research notebook with walk-forward splits, a signal file (ticker, side, size, stop) emitted by deterministic code, an optional Claude 'analyst' pass that annotates/vetoes signals via MCP data tools, and a Lumibot or alpaca-py executor pointed at paper-api.alpaca.markets with kill-switch and max-exposure checks. Log every LLM input/output with timestamps to audit for look-ahead leakage before trusting any backtest that included LLM decisions.

research.summary: For multi-day swing horizons the only approach with strong, replicated, peer-reviewed evidence is cross-sectional ranking of stocks using engineered price/volume features (momentum, reversal, volatility, liquidity) fed to gradient-boosted trees or small neural nets; realistic published out-of-sample numbers are tiny R² (~0.3-0.5% monthly per stock) that still translate to gross long-short Sharpe ~0.8-1.35 value-weighted, with Avramov et al. showing 60-80% of that profit disappears once microcaps, distressed names and trading costs are excluded. The CNN-on-chart-images result (Jiang-Kelly-Xiu, JF 2023) is the one deep-learning result with strong evidence, but its best numbers rely on weekly rebalancing with 600-700% monthly turnover; LSTM/transformer sequence regression and zero-shot time-series foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos) have repeatedly failed to beat linear or random-walk baselines on returns (they do help for volatility forecasting). Regime detection (HMM/GARCH) is useful as a risk filter but suffers label switching and must use filtered, not smoothed, probabilities; classical chart-pattern detection (head-and-shoulders, candlesticks) has 25 years of evidence showing marginal information content and no stand-alone profitability. LLM news sentiment shows real but short-lived, short-leg-dominated, cost-sensitive predictability (Lopez-Lira & Tang: Sharpe 3.28 gross, unprofitable at 20 bps round-trip) and is contaminated by lookahead bias whenever the backtest overlaps the model's training window. The methodology literature (Deflated Sharpe Ratio, PBO/CSCV, combinatorial purged CV, t>3 hurdle, 26%/58% post-sample/post-publication decay, -30%/-55% delisting returns) is well developed and the tooling (skfolio, pypbo, LightGBM 4.7, XGBoost 3.4) is current; a solo builder should start with GBM-on-features plus a volatility regime filter under a strict walk-forward/CPCV protocol and avoid sequence deep learning, chart-pattern libraries, and LLM-agent frameworks as alpha sources.

Goel, Pasricha, Magris & Kanniainen (arXiv 2505.11163, May 2025): TimesFM fine-tuned with incremental learning statistically outperforms traditional econometric models for realized volatility forecasting (Diebold-Mariano / Giacomini-White tests) — volatility, not returns, is where TSFMs show value.

Verma, Putri & Lesupi (arXiv 2605.27848, May 2026): 3-state Gaussian HMM (BIC-selected) on SPY/TLT/GLD daily 2004-2025 identifies low-vol/transitional/high-vol regimes; HMM-based and RL allocations beat passive SPY with lower drawdowns, using a 30% out-of-sample window and one-day execution lag. Abstract gives no Sharpe numbers (a secondary summary cites Sharpe 1.22 / 19.5% max DD vs SPY 55% DD — unverified).

Boukardagha, 'Explainable Regime Aware Investing' (arXiv 2603.04441, Feb 2026): in strictly causal rolling estimation HMMs suffer label switching across windows, drifting optimal regime count, and turnover amplification; regime-identity stability is 'a first-order determinant of portfolio drawdown'. Proposed fix is a causal Wasserstein-HMM that tracks component identity.

Regime labels must be computed from filtered probabilities (data up to current bar); smoothed probabilities use the full sample and make historical regimes look cleaner than achievable live — a common look-ahead leak in HMM backtests.

Three-state Gaussian HMM across five Asian indices with a Jan-2022 cutoff (4-year OOS): hybrid regime strategy beat buy-and-hold on Sharpe in 3 of 5 markets (Nikkei 225 0.71 vs 0.47; STI 0.84 vs 0.53).
Tooling: hmmlearn 0.3.3 (2024-10-31; GaussianHMM etc.), arch 8.0.0 (2025-10-21; ARCH/GARCH/TARCH/EGARCH/EWMA).

facts.claim: Lopez-Lira & Tang (arXiv 2304.07619): 134,129 headlines, 4,106 firms, Oct 2021-Dec 2023; GPT-4 headline scores give a long-short strategy of 38 bps/day, annualized Sharpe 3.28, >650% cumulative gross; short leg does most of the work (29 bps/day, Sharpe 2.12 vs long 9 bps, 0.90); cumulative return falls to >300% at 5 bps round-trip, 150% at 10 bps and the strategy is unprofitable at 20 bps; 81% of headlines are overnight news; GPT-3.5 Sharpe 1.79, older models negative.

Glasserman & Lin (arXiv 2309.17322, Sep 2023): removing company identifiers from headlines ('anonymization') improves in-sample GPT sentiment trading, implying 'distraction' from the LLM's general firm knowledge outweighs look-ahead bias, strongest for large companies; anonymization is recommended for both backtests and live use.

Gao, Jiang & Yan, 'Detecting Lookahead Bias in LLM Forecasts' (arXiv 2512.23847, Dec 2025, rev. Jun 2026): Lookahead Propensity (LAP) is materially positive in-sample and collapses to zero after the training cutoff; LLM return forecasts are more accurate exactly where LAP is high, indicating contamination of in-window backtests including the Lopez-Lira & Tang result.

He, Lv, Manela & Wu, 'Chronologically Consistent Large Language Models' (arXiv 2502.21206, 2025): ChronoBERT/ChronoGPT trained only on point-in-time text achieve next-day news-return Sharpe ratios comparable to a much larger Llama model, so the lookahead-bias penalty is modest for that specific task and 'model and application-specific'.

Benhenda, 'Look-Ahead-Bench' (arXiv 2601.13770, Jan 2026): standard LLMs (Llama 3.1, DeepSeek 3.2) show alpha decay across the training cutoff (secondary summary: DeepSeek 3.2 +20.7% annualized alpha in-sample to -1.0% out-of-sample; Llama 3.1 8B +13.8% to -3.4%), while point-in-time 'Pitinf' models do not.

Kelly, Malamud, Schwab & Xu, 'Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models' (arXiv 2607.11889, Apr/Jul 2026): 4B-parameter decoder trained on 1T chronologically filtered tokens 2013-2024 approaches Gemma-3-4B / LLaMA-7B on reasoning benchmarks, providing leak-free LLMs for backtesting.

Chen, Kelly & Xiu, 'Expected Returns and Large Language Models' (SSRN 2023): contextual LLM embeddings of newswire text predict returns across 16 equity markets and 13 languages; prices assimilate news with an exploitable delay and 'fresh news alerts' give higher Sharpe ratios. Specific Sharpe figures not verifiable from accessible sources.

Ye et al., 'The Alpha Illusion' (arXiv 2605.16895, May 2026): re-evaluates FinMem, TradingAgents, FinAgent, QuantAgent, FLAG-Trader; argues reported LLM-agent Sharpe ratios cannot be separated from temporal contamination, unmodeled frictions and short-window Sharpe uncertainty. Secondary summaries report TradingAgents Sharpe 0.43 to 0.22 after costs and underperforming buy-and-hold on 4 of 5 stocks, and >50% performance drops for FinMem/QuantAgent after the training cutoff.

Bailey & Lopez de Prado, 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio', Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5):94-107 (2014): corrects a backtested Sharpe for selection under multiple trials and non-normality; inputs are number of trials, variance of trial Sharpe ratios, skewness, kurtosis, and sample length.

Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado & Zhu, 'The Probability of Backtest Overfitting' (Journal of Computational Finance): CSCV procedure estimates the probability that the in-sample-best strategy underperforms out-of-sample; implemented in R package pbo and Python pypbo (PBO, performance degradation, probabilistic Sharpe).
Harvey, Liu & Zhu (NBER w20592 / RFS 2016): because of multiple testing, a new return predictor should clear t > 3.0 rather than 2.0.
McLean & Pontiff (JF 2016), 97 published predictors: returns decline 26% out-of-sample (after sample end, pre-publication) and 58% post-publication (0.58% to 0.26% monthly).

Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley 2018) defines purged k-fold with embargo and Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV), plus the 'seven sins' (Sisyphus paradigm, integer differentiation, inefficient sampling, wrong labeling, non-IID weighting, CV leakage, backtest overfitting); Arnott, Harvey & Markowitz, 'A Backtesting Protocol in the Era of Machine Learning' (JFDS 2019) gives a research protocol against self-deception.

CPCV tooling: skfolio 1.4.11 (2026-10-03) ships CombinatorialPurgedCV(n_folds, n_test_folds) and WalkForward; temporalcv provides PurgedKFold with purge_gap and embargo; mlfinlab is closed-source/paid and its free fork unmaintained since 2018.

Trading costs: Frazzini, Israel & Moskowitz measured median institutional cost of 6.24 (NYSE) / 6.16 (Nasdaq) bps per rebalance 1998-2013; Novy-Marx & Velikov (RFS 2016) use Hasbrouck effective spreads and find few anomalies with >50% monthly turnover survive costs; academic ML papers (Jiang-Kelly-Xiu) assume 10 bps for stocks above the 80th NYSE size percentile and 20 bps otherwise.

recommendations: START HERE (tier 1): cross-sectional ranking model. Engineer ~30-100 stock-level features (1-12 month momentum, 1-week/1-month reversal, realized and idiosyncratic volatility, dollar volume, Amihud illiquidity, 52-week-high distance, volume shocks) on a liquid, survivorship-free universe; train LightGBM/XGBoost (and optionally a small 2-3 layer MLP) to predict 5-20 day forward return RANK, not price level. Expect monthly R²oos of ~0.3-0.5% and gross value-weighted long-short Sharpe ~0.8-1.3 in-paper (GKX), and plan for Avramov-style haircuts of 60%+ once microcaps and costs are removed. This is the only approach with multiple independent peer-reviewed replications.

Tier 1 methodology, non-negotiable: walk-forward (expanding window, retrain yearly) plus skfolio CombinatorialPurgedCV with purge = label horizon and embargo; log every trial and compute the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (pypbo or your own) with the true trial count; require DSR-significance and a t-stat > 3 before trusting a strategy; charge at least 10 bps per side for large caps and 20 bps otherwise plus spread; assume 26-58% decay from published/backtested numbers (McLean-Pontiff); use delisting-adjusted data (-30%/-55% fallback returns) and point-in-time constituents.

Tier 2 (add second): volatility/regime filter as a risk overlay, not a predictor. GARCH or realized-vol thresholds (arch 8.0) or a 2-3 state Gaussian HMM (hmmlearn 0.3.3) fitted on rolling windows, using FILTERED probabilities with a one-day lag, used to scale gross exposure or halt new entries in high-vol regimes. Guard against label switching by anchoring states to their volatility ordering each refit (Boukardagha 2026). Evaluate by drawdown reduction, not by added return.

Tier 3 (optional, after tier 1 is live): replicate Jiang-Kelly-Xiu CNN-on-images using their published replication code at the 20-day horizon only (weekly rebalancing needs 600-700% monthly turnover). Benchmark it against a logistic regression on devolatized returns first — the paper itself shows that is competitive at 60-day histories — and expect post-2019 decay since no independent 2020-2026 out-of-sample replication was found.

Tier 3 (optional): LLM news sentiment as an overlay. Only use data after the model's training cutoff (or a point-in-time model such as ChronoGPT/Pitinf), anonymize tickers and company names in prompts (Glasserman-Lin), and remember the Lopez-Lira & Tang alpha is mostly in the SHORT leg, overnight, and dies at 20 bps round-trip — so for a long-biased retail swing book treat it as a veto/filter on entries rather than a standalone signal.

AVOID as alpha sources: (1) LSTM/transformer/TSFM regression on price sequences — directional accuracy ~50%, worse than linear baselines, foundation models beat random walk only sparsely; use Chronos-2/TimesFM only for volatility forecasting if at all. (2) Classical chart-pattern and candlestick detection (TA-Lib CDL*, PatternPy, stock-pattern) as entry signals — 25 years of evidence shows marginal information content and no stand-alone profitability; at most use detector outputs as additional GBM features and let the model decide. (3) LLM trading-agent frameworks (FinMem, TradingAgents, QuantAgent, FLAG-Trader) — reported Sharpes collapse after costs and after the training cutoff. (4) Any backtest that uses random (non-chronological) CV, current index constituents, globally normalized features, or smoothed HMM states.

Architecture implication for the user's 'AI swing trader': keep the LLM out of the signal path. Use it as an auditable information interface (news parsing, feature extraction, code generation, report writing) upstream of a deterministic, independently validated GBM ranking model, a regime risk overlay, and an execution module — the same separation recommended by the Alpha Illusion paper.

research.summary: A Claude-based swing-trading system should be built as a layered pipeline in which every number (scan, features, model score, backtest stats, position size, order parameters) is produced by deterministic Python code exposed as tools, and Claude is confined to the language/judgment layer: reading filings, news, and congressional disclosures, scoring candidates against an explicit rubric via structured outputs, explaining setups, and writing/iterating strategy code in a separate dev loop. The 2025-2026 research literature (STOCKBENCH, PriceSeer, Agent Trading Arena, "The Alpha Illusion") consistently finds that LLMs underperform buy-and-hold as end-to-end traders, reason poorly over plain-text numbers, are fooled by fake news, and that reported LLM-trading alpha is inflated by temporal contamination and unmodeled costs; the same papers recommend exactly this modular design. Verified MCP servers exist for Alpaca (official, paper trading on by default), Alpha Vantage (official, mcp.alphavantage.co), Financial Datasets (official), Webull (official cloud + local server with built-in order caps), Interactive Brokers (community, alpha), and Quiver Quant (official claude.ai connector requiring an API subscription, plus a community server). "Liquid Trade" (liquid.trade) is a non-custodial perpetual-futures DEX aggregator with a Co-Invest MCP server, not a securities broker; its synthetic equity perps, up to 50x leverage, and unstated jurisdiction/KYC rules make it unsuitable as the broker for a US stock swing-trading system without legal review. The Claude Agent SDK provides the governance primitives needed (PreToolUse hooks that deny even in bypass mode, canUseTool human-approval callback, allowed/disallowed tool lists, PostToolUse audit hooks), and daily Claude cost is small (roughly $0.15-0.30 per 20-name review on Sonnet 5.5/Opus 5.5, i.e. low single-digit to low tens of dollars per month), so data and broker subscriptions dominate the budget.

Claude Agent SDK (Python `pip install claude-agent-sdk`, TypeScript `npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) provides built-in file/bash/web tools, hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions, sessions, and auto-loads skills from .claude/; third-party products must use API-key auth, not claude.ai login.

Agent SDK permission evaluation order is: Hooks -> deny rules -> ask rules -> permission mode -> allow rules -> canUseTool callback. A PreToolUse hook deny applies even in bypassPermissions; `disallowed_tools=['Bash']` removes the tool definition entirely; allow-list wildcards are only valid after a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix; modes are default, dontAsk, acceptEdits, bypassPermissions, plan, auto.

PreToolUse hooks return `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` of 'allow' | 'deny' | 'ask' | 'defer' with `permissionDecisionReason` and optional `updatedInput`; 'defer' ends the turn with stop_reason 'tool_deferred' so the process can exit and resume later; PostToolUse hooks can log every call for audit; PermissionRequest/Notification hooks can push approval requests to Slack; matchers support `^mcp__` regex to cover all MCP tools.

The canUseTool callback (Python `ClaudeAgentOptions(can_use_tool=...)`, returning `PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...)` or `PermissionResultDeny(message=...)`; TypeScript `{behavior:'allow', updatedInput}` / `{behavior:'deny', message}`) is the human-approval gate; it never fires for tools auto-approved by allow rules or modes, so order-placing tools must not be in allowed_tools.

Agent SDK MCP config: `mcp_servers={name: {command, args, env}}` for stdio or `{type:'http', url, headers}` for remote; tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; MCP tools require explicit permission (allowed_tools) before Claude can call them; in-process SDK MCP servers let you define custom tools in your own code; the SDK does not run interactive OAuth flows (pass a bearer token in headers).

MCP spec (2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25): 'there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations'; clients SHOULD prompt for confirmation on sensitive operations, show tool inputs before calling, validate results, implement timeouts, and log tool usage; clients MUST treat tool `annotations` (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) as untrusted unless from trusted servers.

STOCKBENCH (arXiv 2510.02209): in a contamination-free multi-month trading benchmark with daily prices, fundamentals and news, most state-of-the-art LLM agents underperformed simple buy-and-hold; strong financial QA performance 'does not necessarily translate into effective trading behavior'.

'The Landscape of LLM Trading Agents' / 'The Alpha Illusion' (arXiv 2605.16895): reported LLM-trading performance is inflated by temporal contamination (performance drops >50% on post-training data), unmodeled friction (a TradingAgents reproduction's Sharpe fell from 0.43 to 0.22 with realistic costs), and short evaluation windows; the authors recommend modular architectures where LLMs extract information upstream while quantitative methods handle calibration, risk and execution.

PriceSeer (arXiv 2601.06088): a live, data-uncontaminated benchmark of 110 US stocks found top LLMs can exceed 0.5 hit rate short-term but show 'vulnerability to fake news' and 'suboptimal performance in long-term predictions'.

Agent Trading Arena (arXiv 2502.17967): 'LLMs struggle with numerical reasoning when given plain-text data, often overfitting to local patterns and recent values', while chart-image inputs and a reflection step materially improve numerical reasoning and trading outcomes.

recommendations: Architecture: four layers. (1) Data layer: Alpaca (broker + bars + news, paper by default) or IBKR/Webull, Alpha Vantage or Financial Datasets for fundamentals/indicators, Quiver for congressional/insider/lobbying/dark-pool data, an EDGAR MCP for filing text; persist everything to a local store (DuckDB/Postgres) so backtests and the live loop read identical data. (2) Quant layer in plain Python: universe scan, feature computation (pandas/TA-Lib/pandas-ta), ML scoring (LightGBM/sklearn), backtests (vectorbt or NautilusTrader), ATR-based position sizing, portfolio/risk checks. (3) Claude layer: reads text, applies a rubric, returns structured JSON. (4) Governance layer: Agent SDK hooks, approval callback, audit log, kill switch.

Expose every quant function to Claude as a tool (an in-process SDK MCP server or Skill scripts) and make the rule explicit in the system prompt and in the rubric schema: Claude never emits a price target, a share count, a dollar size, or a backtest statistic; it emits categorical/ordinal judgments and cites which tool output supports each one. Because structured outputs cannot enforce minimum/maximum on numbers, validate every numeric field client-side and reject the response if it contains numbers not traceable to a tool result.

Use structured outputs (`output_config.format` json_schema, or `strict: true` tools) for the review step with a fixed schema such as: ticker, thesis (<=2 sentences), catalyst_within_hold_window (bool), event_risk_flags (enum list: earnings_within_N_days, pending_8K, guidance_cut, litigation, dilution), news_contradicts_setup (bool), congressional_or_insider_signal (enum), liquidity_concern (bool), rubric_scores (0-5 per criterion), decision (approve_for_risk_check | reject | needs_more_info), evidence (list of tool_call ids/URLs). Threshold the scores deterministically in code, not in the prompt.

Daily loop (pre-market, cron or Managed Agents scheduled deployment): scan.py -> features.py -> score.py produce shortlist.json; Claude (Sonnet 5.5 at low/medium effort, or Haiku 4.5 for first-pass summarization) reviews each candidate with news/filings/Quiver context and the rubric; risk.py computes size, stop, target, portfolio exposure, correlation and the daily-loss budget; the order tool is gated by canUseTool so a human approves each ticket (push via a PermissionRequest/Notification hook to Slack; use the PreToolUse 'defer' decision if approval may take hours); orders go out as bracket/limit orders; PostToolUse logs every call; after close Claude writes the trade journal entry and a daily explanation.

Where Claude adds value: reading 8-K/10-Q/earnings-call text and news for catalysts and contradictions; summarizing and classifying congressional, insider, lobbying and contract disclosures; detecting event risk the scanner cannot see; explaining each setup in plain language for the journal; generating and iterating strategy and pattern-detector code in a separate Claude Code/Agent SDK dev loop against the backtest harness; reviewing rendered chart images as a secondary sanity check (vision helps per Agent Trading Arena). Where Claude must not be in the loop: predicting prices or returns, position sizing, stop/target math, computing any backtest metric, deciding order parameters, or overriding a deterministic risk veto.

Pattern-recognition overhaul: implement patterns deterministically (TA-Lib's 61 CDL* functions plus custom breakout/consolidation/relative-strength detectors), label a validation set, and have Claude write and iterate the detector code and unit tests against that set in the dev loop; log precision/recall per pattern. Treat any LLM 'does this chart look like X' call as advisory metadata, never as the trigger.

Guardrails to implement in code, not prompts: (a) paper trading only until N weeks of forward results exist, with ALPACA_PAPER_TRADE=true and separate paper keys; (b) a kill-switch file/flag checked by a PreToolUse hook that denies all order tools (hook denies apply even in bypassPermissions); (c) max daily loss and max drawdown computed from broker account P&L before any order and enforced in the order tool itself; (d) per-order notional cap, per-position cap, max open positions, sector cap, and a symbol allow-list enforced in your own order wrapper (mirror Webull's WEBULL_MAX_ORDER_NOTIONAL_USD / SYMBOL_WHITELIST pattern); (e) put close_all_positions and cancel_all_orders in disallowed_tools in the production loop; (f) never put order tools in allowed_tools so they always reach canUseTool; (g) append-only audit log of prompt hash, tool calls, tool results, model id, and decision, written by PostToolUse hooks.

Follow the Alpha Illusion protocols when evaluating the LLM layer: Claude's training data covers history up to its cutoff, so any backtest where Claude reads news from before the cutoff is contaminated; evaluate the review layer only on forward paper-trading data (or data after the model's cutoff), model commissions/spread/slippage, and treat sub-year Sharpe differences as noise.

Model choice and cost control: run the daily review on Sonnet 5.5 (or Opus 5.5 at medium effort) with the system prompt, rubric, schema and tool definitions in a cached prefix (>=512 tokens, 1-hour TTL for the pre-market window); use Haiku 4.5 for bulk news summarization; use Opus 5.5 for the weekly strategy-code iteration; consider the Batch API (50% off) for the overnight pre-scan only if a multi-hour turnaround is acceptable. Expect low single-digit to low tens of dollars per month in Claude spend; data subscriptions (Alpaca Algo Trader Plus $99, Alpha Vantage $49.99+, Financial Datasets $200, Quiver ~$30) will dominate.

For a baseline 'fully able to access stock data' program: connect the Agent SDK (Python) to alpaca-mcp-server (stdio, paper keys), alphavantage-mcp or the Financial Datasets server, the community Quiver server with QUIVER_API_TOKEN (the official Quiver MCP is a claude.ai connector, not a documented SDK endpoint), and an EDGAR MCP; set allowed_tools to the read-only mcp__ tools only; write a scan/feature/backtest package with scripts exposed as a Skill; run it in paper mode. Credentials must be supplied by you as env vars; the agent should never be given live keys until the paper phase is complete.

Do not use Liquid (liquid.trade) as the broker for this system: it trades synthetic perpetuals (not shares) with leverage up to 50x on a non-custodial DEX aggregator, publishes no jurisdiction/KYC terms on its site, and its Co-Invest MCP is designed for conversational trade proposals. If you still want it connected, use the 'read' scope only for research and get legal confirmation on US-person eligibility first.

Prefer the official MCP servers (Alpaca, Alpha Vantage, Financial Datasets, Webull, Quiver) over community ones; treat the IBKR community server as alpha-quality and, if IBKR is required, consider calling the Client Portal Web API directly from your own in-process SDK MCP tools so the order path is code you control.

refuted_or_doubtful.claim: Alpaca docs (cited in frameworks/llmagent): orders that would flag an account as a Pattern Day Trader are rejected with HTTP 403, and accounts under $25,000 equity are restricted from day trades; 4x intraday buying power requires $25k.
refuted_or_doubtful.problem: Stale. The SEC approved FINRA's amendments to Rule 4210 on April 14, 2026; FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10 sets the effective date at June 4, 2026 (member phase-in allowed until October 20, 2027). The PDT designation, day-trade counting, day-trading buying power and the $25,000 minimum are eliminated and replaced by 'intraday margin deficit' standards. Alpaca's own blog (published April 27, 2026, updated June 4, 2026) says it removed the PDT flag, $25k requirement and day-trade counting, unrestricted previously flagged accounts, replaced Day Trade Buying Power with Intraday Buying Power and Day Trade Margin Calls with Intraday Margin Calls (repeated failures within 5 business days can trigger a 90-day restriction), lowered the threshold for 4x intraday buying power to $2,000 for leverage-enabled accounts, and removed deprecated PDT API fields by July 6, 2026.
refuted_or_doubtful.correction: Design around the new intraday-margin regime, not PDT: a swing system that occasionally exits same-day (stop hit) no longer risks a PDT flag, but it must respect Alpaca's real-time pre-trade intraday margin checks and the $2,000 minimum for margin/short features; do not read deprecated PDT fields from the account endpoint. TAX - Wash-sale rule and trader tax status were not covered: short-term swing gains are taxed as ordinary income; the wash-sale rule (IRC 1091) continues to apply to traders unless a Section 475(f) mark-to-market election is in force, and that election must be filed by the original due date of the prior year's return (e.g., by 2027-04-15 to cover tax year 2027); IRS Topic 429 lists the 'trader in securities' tests (profit from daily movements, substantial, continuous and regular). A system holding 5-20 days across a repeated universe will generate many wash sales; the backtester should at least log them, and any comparison to buy-and-hold should be after-tax. https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc429

COST - Regulatory transaction fees are absent from every cost model: SEC Section 31 fee is $20.60 per $1,000,000 of sales effective 2026-04-04 (FY2026 rate; $0.00 before that date this fiscal year), and FINRA's Trading Activity Fee for covered equity sales is $0.000195 per share with a $9.79 per-trade cap since 2026-01-01. Small, but they are real, sell-side-only and must be in the cost model alongside half-spread and slippage. https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/fee-rate-advisories/2026-2 ; https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rule-filings/sr-finra-2024-019/fee-adjustment-schedule

DATA SOURCE - Free primary sources behind Quiver's paid datasets were never listed: House PTRs are public at https://disclosures-clerk.house.gov/FinancialDisclosure (PDF), Senate PTRs at https://efdsearch.senate.gov/search/ (structured web forms), Form 4 filings at SEC EDGAR (free, structured XML, full-text search at efts.sec.gov), FINRA Daily Short Sale Volume Files (free, posted by 6:00 pm ET same day at https://www.finra.org/finra-data/browse-catalog/reg-sho-daily - this is the raw input to Quiver's 'off-exchange' DPI metric), Lobbying Disclosure Act filings via the free LDA API (API key registration required, https://lda.gov/api/), and federal contract awards via the free, keyless USAspending API v2 (https://api.usaspending.gov/). Quiver sells parsing and convenience, not exclusive data; a solo developer can defer the $30-75/mo until a signal is proven.

DATA SOURCE - Evidence for the alt-data the user asked about: congressional-trade copy strategies have no peer-reviewed post-STOCK-Act alpha (Belmont et al. NBER w26975: senators' buys underperform industry peers by 11-28 bps; Eggers & Hainmueller 2013: no outperformance) and arrive 30-45 days late, whereas opportunistic Form 4 insider buys earn ~82 bps/month value-weighted abnormal returns (Cohen-Malloy-Pomorski, JF 2012). The ML section flagged this as open; it should drive which Quiver tier (if any) is bought. https://www.nber.org/papers/w26975 ; https://www.nber.org/papers/w16454.pdf

DATA SOURCE - Earnings/event calendar: the Claude rubric uses 'earnings_within_N_days' but no section names a source. Alpha Vantage EARNINGS_CALENDAR (function=EARNINGS_CALENDAR, horizon=3month|6month|12month, CSV, one call per day fits the free 25 req/day tier) or EODHD's Corporate Events Calendar & News add-on ($19.99/mo) / Fundamentals feed ($59.99/mo). Also needed: ex-dividend dates and splits for open positions (Alpaca corporate-actions endpoint or EODHD). https://www.alphavantage.co/documentation/

DATA SOURCE - Point-in-time universe membership: EODHD's S&P/Dow Jones Historical Constituents API is a $29.99/mo add-on (S&P 500 membership changes from January 2000), separate from the $19.99 EOD plan; Sharadar (Nasdaq Data Link) is survivorship-free back to 1998 with delisted tickers but its current price was not verified. Alpaca's assets endpoint is current-only. https://eodhd.com/financial-apis/sp-and-dow-jones-indices-historical-constituents-data-api ; https://quantrocket.com/sharadar

METHODOLOGY - Trading calendar and time handling: no section mentions exchange holidays, early closes (1:00 pm ET) or DST-safe scheduling. Use pandas_market_calendars 5.5.0 (MIT, Python >=3.10) for NYSE sessions, keep all timestamps in America/New_York, and schedule the pre-market job relative to the session open rather than fixed UTC. https://pypi.org/pypi/pandas_market_calendars/json

The llmagent kill-switch is good but incomplete without these.

METHODOLOGY - Research-protocol specifics still unspecified: exact label (forward N-day return rank or triple-barrier), per-date cross-sectional normalization of features, embargo >= label horizon, a pre-registered strategy spec with a trial log (needed for the Deflated Sharpe Ratio), explicit baselines (SPY buy-and-hold, 12-1 momentum, equal-weight universe), retraining cadence and model versioning, drift monitoring, minimum forward-test gate (e.g., >= 3 months of paper trading and >= 100 closed trades with costs) and a pre-defined live kill criterion (max drawdown or rolling-Sharpe threshold). 6. Research: vectorbt 1.1.1 (Python 3.11-3.14) + LightGBM 4.7 cross-sectional rank model on ~30-100 price/volume features over a liquid survivorship-free universe; skfolio CombinatorialPurgedCV with purge/embargo = horizon; pypbo for PBO + Deflated Sharpe with the logged trial count; t > 3 hurdle; charge 10/20 bps per side plus fees; benchmark vs SPY buy-and-hold and 12-1 momentum; regime overlay from arch GARCH / hmmlearn with filtered (not smoothed) probabilities.
7. Live engine: plain Python (or Lumibot 4.6.4 on Alpaca) with deterministic risk.py: vol-targeted sizing with per-name/sector caps, mandatory stop, daily-loss and drawdown limits, kill-switch file, settled-cash tracking (T+1, GFV rules) if cash account, start-of-run reconciliation, retries, heartbeat alerts.
8. Claude layer (Agent SDK): Haiku 4.5 for bulk news/filing summarization, Sonnet 5.5 for the daily structured-output rubric review (cached prefix, 1-hour TTL), Opus 5.5 for weekly strategy-code iteration; MCP servers: alpacahq/alpaca-mcp-server (paper default), Quiver official https://mcp.quiverquant.com/ via bearer header (if subscribed), an EDGAR MCP; LLM never emits prices, sizes, stops or backtest stats.

10. Gates: >= 3 months paper and >= 100 closed trades with modeled costs before live; pre-defined live kill criterion; decide the Section 475(f) election by the prior-year filing deadline and log wash sales.
11. Exclusions: no Liquid (liquid.trade) as an equity venue (unregistered perp-DEX aggregator, synthetic 'stocks', up to 50x); no LSTM/transformer/TSFM return forecasting, no chart-pattern libraries as entry triggers, no end-to-end LLM trading agents.
